title: The difficulty resolved: grace of justification taken widely and strictly
source_text: XXXIII. Ad solvendam hanc difficultatem observandum est, apud Protestantes gratiam regenerationis & justificationis modo latius, modo strictius sumi. Ex Protestantium sensu, justificatio stricte & praecise accepta, non est aliud quam hominis peccatoris absolutio, propter Christi satisfactionem ipsi donatam atque imputatam, & sic concipitur ut beneficium distinctum a fide, per quam simus illius participes, & quae ideo fides justificans vocatur. Sub gratia vero justificationis, si latius sumatur, includitur ipsa fides per quam justificamur. Hoc sensu sumunt Protestantes justificationem, quum negant ulla opera vere bona illam antecedere. Idem enim cum ipsis est antecedere justificationem quod antecedere fidem justificantem. Nihilque eatenus justificationem praecedit, quod non fidem etiam praecedat. Adeoque quum dicunt omnia quae fiunt ante justificationem, non esse bona opera, sed peccata, non aliud sibi volunt, quam ante fidem nullum bonum opus in homine existere posse, sed omnia infidelium opera esse peccata.
pass_a_gloss: XXXIII. For solving this difficulty it is to be observed, that among the Protestants the grace of regeneration and of justification is taken sometimes more widely, sometimes more strictly. In the Protestants' sense, justification strictly and precisely taken, is not other than the absolution of the sinful man, on account of Christ's satisfaction given and imputed to him, and so is conceived as a benefit distinct from faith, through which we are partakers of it, and which therefore is called justifying faith. But under the grace of justification, if it be taken more widely, is included the very faith through which we are justified. In this sense the Protestants take justification, when they deny that any works truly good precede it. For it is the same with them to precede justification as to precede justifying faith. And nothing so far precedes justification, as does not also precede faith. And so when they say that all things which are done before justification, are not good works, but sins, they mean nothing else, than that before faith no good work can exist in man, but that all the works of unbelievers are sins.
pass_b_english: Thesis XXXIII. To solve this difficulty we must note that the Protestants use 'the grace of regeneration and justification' sometimes in a wider and sometimes in a stricter sense. In their usage, justification taken strictly and precisely is nothing but the absolution of a sinner for the sake of Christ's satisfaction, which is given and imputed to him. Understood in this way it is a benefit distinct from faith, the faith by which we share in it and which is therefore called justifying faith.

Taken more widely, though, the grace of justification includes the very faith by which we are justified. This is the sense the Protestants have in mind when they deny that any truly good works precede justification. For them, to come before justification is the same as to come before justifying faith, and nothing precedes justification that does not also precede faith.

So when they say that everything done before justification is sin and not a good work, they mean only that no good work can exist in a man before faith, and that all the works of unbelievers are sins.
